_comment: What each operation costs, in credits. One credit is one cent.
An operation is charged when it costs this instance something to run: a
model call to somebody we pay, or a third party billed per request.
Anything that only touches this instance's own storage is 0, because it
has no marginal cost and charging for it taxed exactly the behaviour the
product wants more of. Abuse control for those is auth.CheckPostRate,
not the price.
Talking to your agent is 0 as well, and that is a product decision rather
than an arithmetic one. The agent is the thing you came for; metering it
meant a new account could not ask a question until it had paid, which is
why there used to be a daily grant of credits here to cancel the charge
back out. Both are gone. What bounds it now is `limit` — a count of runs
a day, which is abuse control and not a price.
A price is what a *fetch* costs. A call the instance answered from
something it already had — a cached forecast, a stored tile — is not
charged; see internal/service/meter.go. So the busier a shared instance
is, the less its callers pay.
`limit` is a hard count per account per day, separate from money and
checked before it. It is the second control for the three operations that
reach a stranger — a price stops somebody who has to pay and does nothing
about a loop, and what a loop spends there is a domain's or a number's
reputation, which no balance repairs.
This is an operator's file. Edit it, or drop a quota.json in the data
directory to override without rebuilding.

operations.label: Travel time between two places
operations.note: routes_eta. Google Routes, 0.48¢ at Essentials ($4.78/1k after 10k free), 0.95¢ at Pro. We ask for traffic, which may bill at Pro — priced to cover it. The op id keeps the old name so an operator's existing override and usage history survive the rename

operations.label: Turn-by-turn directions
operations.note: Google Routes asking for steps and the road's shape, which is more than an ETA and bills higher — 1.45¢ at Enterprise

operations.label: Summarise text
operations.note: Atlas deepseek-v4-flash ($0.14/$0.28 per M). 0.13¢ at the 30k cap — a 23x markup, and far more on a typical call

operations.label: Extract structure from text
operations.note: Atlas deepseek-v4-pro ($1.68/$3.38 per M) because a wrong field is silent. 1.63¢ at the 30k cap, so about 3.7x

operations.label: Classify text
operations.note: Atlas deepseek-v4-flash, output is one word. 0.11¢ at the 30k cap — the cheapest real model call here

operations.label: Translate text
operations.note: Atlas deepseek-v4-flash. Output is as long as the input, so on pro this would cost 4.39¢ at the cap against a 4¢ price — the one loss-making path. On flash, 0.37¢ and a 10x markup

operations.label: App build (AI)
operations.note: Was 100 — a dollar, six times the next most expensive thing on the menu, for less model than an agent run

operations.label: App edit (AI)
operations.note: The model call only. Manual editing at /apps/<slug>/edit is free

operations.label: Text message (per segment)
operations.note: Twilio: about a cent to a US mobile, ~5¢ to a UK one, and charged per 160-character segment. A markup that would be silly on a search is the point here — a text cannot be unsent, and the number's reputation is shared by everybody on the instance. Thirteen cents makes a spam run cost real money before any of the other limits are reached

operations.label: WhatsApp message
operations.note: Billed by Meta per 24-hour conversation rather than per message, so a long reply costs the same as a short one and the second message in a conversation is free to us. Cheaper than a text and with a higher daily limit for that reason — and the window itself is the real limit, since this instance can only message somebody who wrote to it in the last day

operations.label: Run a command
operations.note: A shell command in a container: CPU and memory on this machine, capped per container by SHELL_MEMORY and SHELL_CPUS. One flat price rather than a meter on seconds, because the two ends are an `ls` that costs nothing and a build that costs a minute of a core, and metering the difference would need a second endpoint and a unit — see docs/PRICING.md. Priced low rather than like a browser page, because a coding session is hundreds of commands and 4¢ each would make the loop this exists for unaffordable. No daily count: a priced call is bounded by a balance already, and capping one is a paywall with a safety label on it — see TestOnlyOutboundOrFreeIsCapped. What a count would not have bounded anyway is the idle container, which is memory rather than calls; that is reaped, not priced. Keeping files and reading them is 0, because that is this instance's own storage

operations.label: Browser read
operations.note: A Chromium page load: seconds of CPU and a few hundred MB here, or a hosted browser billed around 1.3-3.8¢ a page. web_fetch is 0 and is the right first try; this is what a page that builds itself in the browser costs

operations.label: Browser screenshot
operations.note: The same page load, plus rendering and storing a PNG. A full-page capture scrolls the whole document, which is why it is not the same price as reading it

operations.label: Send a message
operations.note: One price for sending, wherever it is going. It was two — mail_email for an address outside and mail_send at 0 for one here — and the free one was free on every door: over submission a signed-in account could write to every username on the instance at no cost and no cap. Spam is not a fact about which network the recipient is on. Writing to yourself or to your own agent is not a send and is not charged. The cap and the price are both an operator's: CREDIT_COST_MAIL sets what it costs and MAIL_DAILY_LIMIT how many a day, so a self-hosted instance that does not want either can say so without rebuilding — and one with no Stripe and no x402 is never charged anyway, because quota.Charging is false and Metered follows it
